candidateRows: Accepting naturalism together with evolution is self-defeating because the combination undermines confidence in the cognitive faculties by which it is believed.
This states the argument's overarching conclusion and introduces cognitive-faculty reliability as the mechanism connecting naturalism and evolution to epistemic self-defeat.
After introductory material, Plantinga defines naturalism, distinguishes it from mere atheism, and begins presenting the evolutionary argument against naturalism.
If naturalism and evolution are both true, the probability that human cognitive faculties are reliable is low.
The subsequent defeater argument depends directly on this low-reliability probability premise, making it a necessary foundation of the pro case.
Having explained what cognitive faculties are and what their reliability means, Plantinga begins laying out the argument in premise form.

Recognizing the low probability of reliable faculties under naturalism and evolution defeats belief in their reliability, thereby defeating every faculty-produced belief, including naturalism and evolution themselves.
This is the core inferential chain from the reliability premise to the claimed inability rationally to maintain belief in naturalism combined with evolution.
Immediately after stating the low-reliability premise, Plantinga explains how awareness of it spreads a defeater from faculty reliability to all beliefs those faculties produce.

Under materialist naturalism, evolution selects adaptive neurology and behavior rather than belief truth, so the truth of beliefs generated alongside that neurology is approximately a matter of chance.
This supplies the principal causal and probabilistic justification for the disputed claim that reliable cognition is unlikely given naturalism and evolution.
Following the host's tiger illustration, Plantinga develops a hypothetical-creature account linking materialism, adaptive neural processes, behavior, and belief content.

Theism provides reason to expect generally reliable cognitive faculties because human beings are created in God's image with capacities for knowledge, whereas naturalism supplies no comparable expectation.
The contrast clarifies why the reliability problem is directed specifically at naturalism and why the pro side does not regard evolution alone as epistemically self-defeating.
The host's suggestion that God must function as a guarantor of true beliefs within an evolutionary account.
After the host characterizes God as a guarantor of evolutionary belief reliability, Plantinga qualifies that formulation by comparing theistic and naturalistic expectations.
The evolutionary argument does not conclude that naturalism and evolution are false or improbable; it concludes that their conjunction cannot be rationally accepted.
This precisely fixes the intended conclusion of the argument and prevents the central thesis from being assessed as a claim about truth or objective probability.
Law's question whether the argument concludes that naturalism and evolution are false or unlikely to be true.
At the start of the direct exchange, Law asks Plantinga to clarify whether the intended conclusion concerns truth, probability, or rational belief.
Natural selection appears to favor true-belief-producing mechanisms because organisms with adaptive desires survive when their location beliefs are true and fail when those beliefs are false.
This directly challenges the essential low-reliability premise by proposing a selection mechanism that connects accurate representation to adaptive behavior and survival.
Plantinga's premise that naturalism combined with evolution makes reliable cognitive faculties improbable.
After confirming the argument's epistemic conclusion, Law turns to its first premise and begins a survival-based counterexample involving thirst and beliefs about water locations.
Natural selection can favor adaptive neurological behavior without favoring true belief content, leaving evolved cognitive reliability improbable on naturalism.
This supplies the causal separation between adaptive behavior and semantic truth on which the argument's low-reliability premise substantially depends.
The preceding proposal that survival-directed behavior shows evolution will select mechanisms producing true beliefs.
After an intuitive water-seeking example is offered for truth tracking, Plantinga uses a frog's successful behavior to distinguish adaptive neurology from the truth of associated content.
Conceptual constraints link belief content to its neural and behavioral role, making the adaptively successful true belief the most plausible content.
The objection directly attacks the claimed independence of belief content from adaptive behavior and therefore challenges the argument's key probability premise.
Plantinga's claim that adaptive neurological outputs need bear no truth-conducive relation to the belief contents they determine.
Law grants that selection targets behavior but argues that beliefs cannot be assigned arbitrarily to neural structures, using directed water-seeking as the central case.
The alleged likelihood that adaptive neural structures carry behavior-matching true contents cannot be assumed when materialism and evolution are themselves under examination.
This reply challenges the warrant for Law's truth-content likelihood judgment and preserves the possibility that adaptive structures determine false contents.
Law's contention that behavioral and conceptual constraints make the corresponding true content the most likely belief.
Plantinga accepts the materialist framing provisionally but insists that ordinary intuitions about actual belief attribution cannot establish the needed likelihood under the disputed conjunction.
Even without identifying beliefs with neural structures, their causal and conceptual ties to behavior constrain content enough for selection to favor truth.
The move reformulates the reliability challenge so it does not depend on strict mind-brain identity and reconnects adaptive selection with true content.
Plantinga's objection that Law had not justified assigning behavior-matching contents under materialism and evolution.
Law clarifies that his argument requires only an association between beliefs and neural structures, with behavioral effects helping determine what content can properly be attributed.
Supervenience may fix one particular belief for a neural structure, yet it does not show that the fixed content must correspond to the adaptive action produced.
The distinction between content determination and truth-relevant correspondence blocks Law's proposed route from adaptive behavior to reliable cognition.
Law's revised claim that conceptual and causal constraints connect behavior-producing neural states with truth-favoring contents.
Plantinga grants that materialist supervenience could prevent arbitrary content assignment but denies that this determines a content suitably connected with the resulting action.
If adaptive success is indifferent between true and false content, each belief has roughly even truth odds and a substantially reliable belief set is extremely improbable.
This is the explicit probabilistic bridge from content indifference at the individual-belief level to low overall cognitive reliability under naturalism and evolution.
The challenge that Plantinga must explain why naturalistic evolution is more likely to produce false beliefs than true ones.
Plantinga denies claiming that false beliefs are individually more likely, instead arguing that approximately even odds compound into a very low chance of widespread reliability.
Atheism does not entail naturalism because one may reject gods while accepting mathematical objects, nonnatural properties, or other nonphysical realities.
The distinction narrows the population and worldview actually reached by the evolutionary argument and prevents its conclusion from applying to atheism generally.
The host's suggestion that atheism automatically excludes anything beyond the physical universe and therefore amounts to naturalism.
Asked why an atheist would resist the naturalist label, Law argues that the category is difficult to define and is separable from belief or disbelief in gods.
Naturalism entails atheism but not conversely, and is best understood as denying God or anything sufficiently like God despite unavoidable boundary vagueness.
The definition fixes the intended scope of the argument while acknowledging cases such as Platonism that make naturalism stronger than atheism alone.
Following Law's distinction between atheism and naturalism, Plantinga agrees with its direction and offers a deliberately broad, somewhat vague characterization of naturalism.
Theism plus evolution may generate a parallel skeptical problem when apparently reliable faculties disclose suffering that counts against the very God guaranteeing their reliability.
The objection contests the proposed asymmetry between naturalism and theism by arguing that the theistic alternative can enter an analogous self-undermining skeptical condition.
The pro-side implication that theism combined with evolution avoids the skeptical consequences assigned to naturalism combined with evolution.
Law grants for argument's sake that naturalism and evolution lead to skepticism, then uses suffering and divine moral character to construct a similar problem for theism.
Evidence from suffering may lower the probability of the Christian God but does not by itself establish God's nonexistence, especially within a broader evidential picture.
The reply denies the key premise of Law's parallel-defeater construction by distinguishing adverse evidence from a faculty-delivered conclusion that God does not exist.
Law's claim that reliable faculties reveal suffering-based grounds for denying God and thereby reproduce the naturalist's skeptical predicament.
After introductory remarks about Dawkins, Plantinga answers Law by taking suffering seriously while placing it among multiple considerations rather than treating it as decisive disclosure.
The existence of suffering may count against Christian theism, but it is only one consideration within a much larger evidential picture that includes arguments supporting God’s existence.
This directly answers the proposed symmetry between the EAAN and an evil-based defeater by denying that suffering amounts to a comprehensive deliverance against God.
Law’s claim that apparently strong evidence from evil can place theistic belief in the same skeptical predicament as naturalism.

Plantinga accepts that evil is genuinely perplexing and may lower the probability of Christian theism when isolated, but insists that it must be weighed alongside the broader body of theistic evidence.
If theism and Christianity are true, belief in God can possess sources of warrant independent of arguments inferred from observable features of the world.
Independent warrant is a distinct answer to the parity objection because it denies that theistic rationality stands or falls solely with contested evidential arguments.
Law’s suggestion that theistic believers receive an internal defeater when their faculties appear to disclose evidence against God.

After distinguishing the problem of evil from the total evidence, Plantinga adds that Christian belief, if true, has nonargumentative sources of warrant rather than depending primarily on philosophical proofs.
The EAAN poses an interesting challenge but not an insurmountable one, because a naturalist can explain why unguided evolution would tend to favor true beliefs.
This is Law’s direct bottom-line answer to the debate motion and identifies the central mechanism by which naturalism can resist Plantinga’s low-reliability premise.
Plantinga’s argument that naturalism combined with evolution makes reliable cognitive faculties unlikely and therefore defeats belief in that conjunction.

Law clarifies that the EAAN alleges incoherence rather than directly proving naturalism false, acknowledges its seriousness, and maintains that adaptive selection can still favor truth-conducive cognition.
Even if naturalism produces global skepticism, theism gains no comparative advantage because apparent evidence against God can similarly undercut the theist’s trust in divinely supplied faculties.
The parity argument challenges the dialectical value of the EAAN by contending that its skeptical structure can be reproduced within the rival theistic position.
Plantinga’s presentation of the EAAN as a special self-defeat problem for naturalism and evolution rather than for theism.

Law grants for argument’s sake that naturalists might be trapped in skepticism, then argues that theists face analogous undercutting if their faculties supply strong grounds for denying the God presumed to guarantee them.
Law gives no adequate grounds for assuming that neurology selected for adaptive behavior would also yield true belief content under materialism, naturalism, and evolution.
This directly defends the EAAN’s disputed reliability premise by arguing that Law’s adaptive-behavior account merely imports assumptions derived from the actual cognitive situation.
Law’s proposed naturalistic explanation that unguided evolution tends to favor true beliefs through the neurology producing adaptive behavior.

Plantinga calls the EAAN powerful, characterizes Law’s answer as an unsupported link between adaptive neurology and true content, and rejects reasoning from present self-conceptions to the naturalistic hypothetical.

The problem of evil does not amount to cognitive faculties revealing that God does not exist, since Christians can rationally trust that a loving God has sufficient reasons beyond their understanding.
This rejects Law’s proposed theistic analogue to the EAAN by denying that evil supplies the kind of anti-God faculty deliverance needed to generate a parallel defeater.
Law’s contention that apparently powerful evidence from evil undercuts theism and thereby the theist’s confidence in God-given cognitive faculties.

Using Job and the Christian account of the crucifixion, Plantinga argues that perplexity or anger over suffering is compatible with warranted confidence that God has morally sufficient reasons unavailable to believers.
